case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Confrontation Clause permits Mississippi courts to place a screen between a defendant and a child sexual-abuse complainant without an individualized, case-specific judicial finding that blocking face-to-face confrontation is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child witness.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause), as applied to in-court testimony procedures; and Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) (as described in the record as mandatory “shall” language authorizing a screen for certain child witnesses).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pitts argues that the screen procedure denied him the core Confrontation Clause right to face-to-face confrontation because the trial court treated the Mississippi statute as mandatory and failed to make the constitutionally required, case-specific findings of necessity (i.e., that this particular child would be traumatized by seeing him and that the procedure was necessary to protect her). He contends this is the same kind of legislatively presumed trauma the Supreme Court rejected, and that generalized assumptions about child witnesses cannot substitute for evidence-based, individualized findings on the record. He also argues the Mississippi Supreme Court’s approach conflicts with controlling U.S. Supreme Court precedent and warrants summary reversal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Mississippi argues the proceedings satisfied the essential elements of confrontation (oath, cross-examination, and the jury’s ability to observe the witness), and that the trial court effectively determined the screen was necessary to protect the four-year-old child from trauma. The State further contends any error does not warrant Supreme Court intervention because the evidence of guilt was overwhelming, including other witness testimony, the child’s statements to authorities, and a videotaped forensic interview admitted under state evidentiary rules, making any confrontation issue harmless or at least not cert-worthy.
key_precedents: Ohio v. Roberts, 448 U.S. 56 (1980) (abrogated in part by Crawford v. Washington)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest opposing point, pressed by Justice Alito, is that Craig allows protective measures when they serve an important public policy and preserve oath, cross-examination, and demeanor evidence. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, those reliability features are necessary yet not sufficient: Craig conditions any departure from face-to-face confrontation on an individualized, on-the-record judicial finding of necessity, and Coy rejects substituting a legislative presumption for that case-specific predicate. A minimalist, legitimacy-preserving disposition is therefore to vacate or reverse and remand for Craig-compliant findings rather than bless Mississippi’s “shall” procedure as effectively categorical. Harmless-error considerations may affect remedy on remand, but they cannot supply the missing constitutional predicate in the first instance.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that Craig permits departures from face-to-face confrontation when an important public policy is served and oath, cross-examination, and demeanor evidence remain, but Craig makes those features necessary—not sufficient—without an individualized, on-the-record finding of necessity. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Mississippi’s mandatory “shall” screening, applied without case-specific evidence and findings, is the sort of categorical presumption Coy rejected and cannot substitute for the Sixth Amendment’s procedural guarantee as originally understood. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern reinforces that the legislature cannot redefine the constitutional baseline by replacing a judicial necessity determination with a statutory command. Harmless-error arguments may affect remedy on remand, but they do not supply the missing constitutional predicate required before denying face-to-face confrontation at all.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s best argument is that the screen preserved oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation while advancing the compelling policy of protecting a very young child, so the confrontation interest was substantially satisfied. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Maryland v. Craig makes those reliability features necessary yet insufficient absent an individualized, on-the-record finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the restriction is necessary; Coy likewise rejects legislative generalizations as a substitute for case-specific justification. Treating Mississippi’s statutory “shall” as doing the constitutional work would effectively allow the legislature to displace the judicial necessity inquiry Craig requires, and harmless-error considerations cannot supply the missing predicate finding. Under our settled precedents, the failure to make child-specific findings is a constitutional defect requiring reversal or vacatur and remand for Craig-compliant proceedings.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation preserve much of confrontation and that protecting a four-year-old is a weighty policy interest. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Maryland v. Craig makes those reliability features a backstop, not a substitute for the constitutional predicate: an individualized, on-the-record finding—based on evidence—that this specific child needs this specific restriction and that it is necessary. Coy v. Iowa forecloses treating a screen as a routine, legislature-presumed accommodation; Mississippi’s “shall” rule, applied without child-specific findings, risks normalizing a barrier in the very cases where credibility is central and the defendant’s liberty is on the line. The modest, precedent-faithful course is vacatur or reversal and remand for Craig-compliant findings, with harmless-error issues left for the lower courts in the first instance.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains that Craig allows limited departures from face-to-face confrontation when an important public policy is served and the core reliability features (oath, cross, demeanor) are preserved. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Craig makes an individualized, on-the-record necessity finding the constitutional predicate for invoking that exception; a statutory “shall” applied without child-specific findings collapses Craig into the kind of categorical presumption Coy rejected. Even if the record might support harmlessness, that goes to remedy rather than supplying the missing constitutional procedure in the first instance. The narrow, workable disposition is to vacate/reverse and remand for Craig-compliant findings (with harmless-error addressed below if needed), not to bless a legislative shortcut that rewrites the constitutional baseline.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—emphasized by Justice Alito—is that the procedure retained oath, cross-examination, and the jury’s ability to assess demeanor, thereby preserving Craig’s “essence of effective confrontation.” But Coy and Craig treat those reliability features as necessary yet not sufficient: dispensing with face-to-face confrontation requires a judicial, individualized, on-the-record finding of necessity that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the restriction is needed. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, allowing Mississippi’s statutory “shall” to substitute for that judicial predicate would let the legislature redefine the Sixth Amendment baseline, a separation-of-powers problem as well as a Confrontation Clause violation. Harmless-error arguments, as Justice Kagan observes, may affect remedy on remand but cannot supply the missing constitutional findings required before employing the screen in the first instance.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that the screen preserved oath, cross-examination, and demeanor and served the vital policy of protecting a very young child—has force as a practical matter, and Craig recognizes that important public policies can justify limited departures from face-to-face confrontation. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Craig makes an individualized, on-the-record necessity finding the constitutional predicate for that departure; without it, Mississippi’s mandatory “shall” rule functions as the kind of categorical presumption Coy rejected. Even if the record might support harmlessness, Justice Kagan is right that harmless-error analysis addresses remedy and does not supply the missing Craig finding or validate a procedure applied without the constitutionally required judicial determination. The institutionally narrow course is therefore reversal or vacatur and remand for Craig-compliant findings, preserving precedent and leaving States room to protect child witnesses within constitutional bounds.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains that Craig allows alternatives to face-to-face confrontation when an important public policy is served and the usual reliability features—oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation—are preserved. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Craig makes an individualized, on-the-record finding of necessity the constitutional predicate for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation; a mandatory statutory “shall,” applied without case-specific evidence and findings, is exactly the kind of generalized presumption Coy rejected. On a textualist/originalist reading informed by Craig and Coy, the absence of that judicial necessity determination is a structural Sixth Amendment defect, and harmlessness goes only to remedy, not to whether the procedure complied in the first instance. The narrow, precedent-faithful disposition is reversal or vacatur with remand for Craig-compliant findings rather than validating a legislative shortcut.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Craig allows departures from face-to-face confrontation when an important policy is served and oath/cross/demeanor remain—still does not carry the day because Craig makes an individualized, on-the-record necessity finding the constitutional trigger, not a dispensable formality. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Mississippi’s mandatory “shall” screening, applied without case-specific findings, substitutes legislative generalization for the judicial safeguard Coy and Craig demand, undermining procedural fairness when credibility is central. I agree with Justice Kagan that harmless error is a remedial inquiry and cannot supply the missing constitutional predicate required before the courtroom procedure is implemented. The appropriate course is to reverse or vacate and remand for Craig-compliant findings (with harmlessness left to the lower courts if necessary).

John Roberts.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa held that placing a screen to block a child witness’s view of the defendant is a serious infringement of the Sixth Amendment’s face-to-face confrontation guarantee, and Maryland v. Craig allowed such a departure only upon an individualized, case-specific judicial finding that it is necessary to protect that particular child from trauma. If Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) was treated as mandatory (“shall”) and the trial court made no on-the-record, child-specific necessity finding, the procedure conflicts with Craig’s constitutional prerequisite and cannot be sustained on a generalized legislative presumption. To preserve precedent and institutional legitimacy, the narrow disposition is to reverse (or vacate and remand) for application of Craig’s required individualized findings, leaving broader questions about alternative protective procedures and harmless error for the lower courts in the first instance.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s text secures the accused’s right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” which at minimum includes the ordinary, face-to-face encounter in open court. Under Coy v. Iowa, placing a screen to block the witness’s view of the defendant is a paradigmatic Confrontation Clause violation absent a specific, evidentiary finding of necessity, and Maryland v. Craig permits departure from face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific judicial determination that the procedure is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), as applied with mandatory “shall” language and without individualized findings, substitutes a legislative presumption for the constitutional inquiry Craig demands, and thus cannot override the Confrontation Clause’s original public meaning. Any harmless-error arguments do not cure the structural violation of the confrontation procedure itself where the required necessity finding was never made on the record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Although Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig require a case-specific finding before dispensing with face-to-face confrontation, Craig also makes clear that the Confrontation Clause is satisfied so long as the procedure is necessary to further an important public policy and preserves the “essence of effective confrontation” through oath, cross-examination, and observation of demeanor. Given the child’s very young age (four) and the State’s compelling interest in protecting child sexual-abuse victims, the trial court’s decision to use a screen falls within Craig’s recognized exception, and I am not persuaded this case warrants this Court’s intervention absent a clear, outcome-determinative violation. Moreover, the State’s harmlessness argument—based on other testimony and the videotaped forensic interview admitted under Mississippi evidentiary rules—counsels against granting relief on collateral procedural grounds. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) reflects a practical legislative judgment about protecting vulnerable witnesses, and nothing here shows the procedure undermined the reliability aims of the Sixth Amendment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s ordinary guarantee of face-to-face confrontation may be limited to protect child witnesses only upon an individualized, case-specific judicial finding of necessity, not a categorical, legislature-presumed rule. In Coy v. Iowa, the Court condemned the use of a screen that prevented the child from seeing the defendant absent such findings, and Maryland v. Craig reaffirmed that any departure requires the trial court to hear evidence and determine that the measure is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child and is narrowly tailored. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), as applied with mandatory “shall” language and without an on-the-record, child-specific necessity determination, conflicts with Coy and Craig and risks eroding a core trial right—especially where credibility is central and the vulnerable witness’s protection can be achieved through constitutionally compliant, individualized procedures.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa treats a physical screen that blocks face-to-face confrontation as a paradigmatic Confrontation Clause violation absent a justification, and Maryland v. Craig allows departure from face-to-face confrontation only on a case-specific, on-the-record finding that the measure is necessary to prevent trauma to the particular child witness. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), if applied as mandatory “shall” authorization without individualized judicial findings, effectively substitutes a legislative presumption of trauma for the constitutionally required necessity determination, which Craig expressly forbids. The State’s reliance on oath, cross-examination, and jury observation cannot cure the missing Craig finding because face-to-face confrontation is a “preference” that may be overcome only by a necessity showing; harmless-error arguments go to remedy, not to whether the procedure complied with the Sixth Amendment in the first instance. A workable middle ground consistent with statutory purpose is to permit protective measures for child witnesses, but only after the trial judge makes specific findings tailored to this child and this defendant as Craig requires.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s Confrontation Clause secures a defendant’s right to face-to-face confrontation, and departures from that rule are permissible only upon a judicial, case-specific finding of necessity. Coy v. Iowa held that using a screen to prevent the witness from seeing the accused is an “obvious” violation absent a constitutionally adequate justification, and Maryland v. Craig allowed an exception only where the trial court “hear[s] evidence” and makes an individualized determination that the procedure is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child. A statute like Miss. Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), read as mandatory “shall” screening without individualized findings, cannot substitute legislative presumption for the judicial determination Craig requires, and permitting it would erode the separation of powers by letting the legislature define away a constitutional guarantee. Whatever the State’s harmless-error arguments, the constitutional rule is clear: no screen absent on-the-record, case-specific necessity findings as Craig demands.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa holds that placing a screen to block a child witness’s view of the defendant is a paradigmatic violation of the Confrontation Clause’s face-to-face guarantee absent a constitutionally sufficient justification. Maryland v. Craig allows a departure from face-to-face confrontation only upon an individualized, case-specific judicial finding of necessity—after hearing evidence—that this particular child would suffer trauma from testifying in the defendant’s presence and that the alternative procedure is necessary to protect the child. If Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) is applied as mandatory “shall” language without those case-specific findings on the record, that rule cannot be squared with Craig’s requirement and risks substituting legislative generalizations for constitutional adjudication. Precedent, workability, and institutional legitimacy favor enforcing Craig’s clear procedural safeguard while leaving States room to protect child witnesses through individualized findings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s Confrontation Clause embodies a core preference for face-to-face confrontation, and this Court has held that any departure from that norm requires a judicially made, individualized finding of necessity. Coy v. Iowa found a screen that prevents the witness from seeing the defendant to be an “obvious” violation absent adequate justification, and Maryland v. Craig allowed an exception only where the trial court “hear[s] evidence” and makes a “case-specific” determination that the procedure is necessary to protect the particular child from trauma. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), as applied here with mandatory “shall” language and without an on-the-record, case-specific necessity finding, substitutes legislative generalization for the constitutionally required judicial determination and thus conflicts with Coy and Craig. Whatever the other confrontation features present (oath, cross-examination, jury observation), Craig makes individualized necessity the predicate for denying face-to-face confrontation, and that predicate is missing here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa holds that a physical barrier preventing a child witness from seeing the defendant violates the Confrontation Clause absent a case-specific showing, rejecting legislatively presumed trauma. Maryland v. Craig permits a departure from face-to-face confrontation only when the trial court makes individualized findings on the record that the procedure is necessary to protect this particular child from trauma caused by the defendant’s presence and that reliability is otherwise assured. Treating Miss. Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) as mandatory “shall” language—without an individualized necessity finding—short-circuits that constitutional prerequisite and undermines procedural fairness in a criminal trial. The State’s reliance on cross-examination and other evidence goes more to harmless-error analysis than to whether the Constitution allows the screen absent Craig’s required findings.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Confrontation Clause permits Mississippi courts to use a mandatory screen that blocks a child witness’s view of the defendant without case-specific, on-the-record findings that the procedure is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause), as applied through the Fourteenth Amendment; and Mississippi’s mandatory child-witness screen statute referenced as Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) (as discussed in the excerpts).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pitts argues the trial court violated the Sixth Amendment by requiring his four-year-old daughter to testify behind a screen that prevented face-to-face confrontation without making the individualized, case-specific necessity finding demanded by Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig. He contends Mississippi treated the screen as mandatory under § 99-43-101(2)(g), effectively replacing Craig’s constitutional prerequisite (necessity shown for this witness) with a categorical legislative presumption of trauma. He further maintains the record lacks evidence that this child would be traumatized by seeing him—indeed, testimony suggested she loved and missed him—so the constitutional standard was not and could not have been satisfied. Because the error is structural or at least not harmless under the governing confrontation framework, he argues certiorari (and even summary reversal) is warranted to enforce clearly established Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Mississippi argues the state courts correctly rejected the Confrontation Clause claim because the proceedings preserved the ‘essential elements’ of confrontation (oath, cross-examination, and jury observation of demeanor) even with the screen in place, and because the trial court determined the screen procedure was necessary to protect the child from trauma. The State also contends the conviction should stand regardless because the evidence of guilt was overwhelming—through multiple witnesses, the child’s statements to authorities, and a recorded forensic interview—so any confrontation-related error was harmless and does not merit Supreme Court review.
key_precedents: Ohio v. Roberts, 448 U.S. 56 (1980) (abrogated on other grounds by Crawford v. Washington)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation preserved confrontation’s functional core and so any deficiency can be treated as harmless—does not answer Coy and Maryland v. Craig’s premise that face-to-face confrontation is the constitutional default and may be denied only after a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Craig treats those reliability features as necessary but not sufficient once the State affirmatively blocks the witness from seeing the accused; allowing Mississippi’s regime to operate as effectively automatic risks converting Craig’s narrow exception into a categorical rule. California v. Green and Kentucky v. Stincer, invoked by Justice Alito, concern different confrontation questions (prior statements and the scope of participation) and do not authorize dispensing with face-to-face confrontation absent Craig’s predicate. A narrow reversal requiring explicit Craig findings before employing this screen best respects precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy without foreclosing child-protection measures supported by individualized evidence.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmlessness-and-functional-safeguards argument does not answer the antecedent constitutional question: whether the State may deny face-to-face confrontation without the case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding Craig requires. The Confrontation Clause’s text, as understood at the founding, secures confrontation with the accused as the default; Coy correctly treated a screen as an “obvious” violation absent a particularized justification, and Mississippi’s effectively mandatory regime replaces that judicial predicate with a legislative presumption. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Craig’s oath/cross/demeanor factors are necessary but not sufficient once the State affirmatively blocks the witness from seeing the defendant, and Green and Stincer do not authorize dispensing with physical confrontation in the first place. Because the trial court never made the requisite necessity determination, the judgment cannot stand on this record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s point that Coy and Craig frame face-to-face confrontation as the default and require case-specific, on-the-record necessity findings before a court may interpose a screen. But under my methodology, Craig’s emphasis on preserving the confrontation “elements of confrontation”—oath, full cross-examination, and the jury’s ability to observe demeanor—matters greatly, and I do not read Craig as making the absence of idealized findings automatically reversible where the procedure plainly served the State’s substantial interest in protecting a very young child and the defense suffered no meaningful impairment in testing the testimony. Justice Kavanaugh’s characterization of the missing finding as “structural” is not compelled by our precedents; we have repeatedly treated confrontation errors as subject to harmless-error review, and I would not constitutionalize an automatic-reversal rule that disregards practical consequences on a record like this. I would affirm, while making clear—consistent with Roberts’s institutional concern—that trial courts must make explicit Craig-compliant findings going forward and that statutes cannot operate as categorical substitutes for judicial necessity determinations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error and “functional core” account (oath, cross, demeanor) does not answer the threshold problem: under Maryland v. Craig, those safeguards are necessary but not sufficient when the State affirmatively denies face-to-face confrontation; the Constitution requires a child-specific, on-the-record necessity finding tied to trauma from the defendant’s presence. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, allowing Mississippi’s regime to operate effectively automatically would convert Craig’s narrow exception into a categorical presumption—the very move Coy condemned—especially troubling in criminal cases where the costs fall on defendants and legitimacy depends on transparent, individualized judicial gating. Even if the evidence seems strong, the absence of the Craig predicate is not a mere technicality; it is the constitutional condition that authorizes the procedure in the first place, so post hoc harmlessness cannot supply what the trial court never found. A narrow reversal requiring proper findings before using a screen protects child witnesses while preserving confrontation’s core protection for vulnerable defendants and the integrity of the adjudicative process.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—endorsing a functional “core” of confrontation through oath, cross-examination, and demeanor evidence plus the State’s child-protection interest—still does not answer Craig’s gating requirement: those safeguards are necessary conditions, not substitutes, when the State affirmatively denies face-to-face confrontation. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Craig and Coy make the constitutional hinge an individualized, on-the-record necessity finding tied to trauma caused by the defendant’s presence; letting Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) operate effectively automatically converts a narrow exception into a categorical presumption. Alito’s reliance on Green and Stincer, as several colleagues note, concerns different confrontation questions and cannot supply authority to bypass Craig’s predicate findings. Even if harmless-error review might be appropriate in some confrontation contexts, it cannot cure the antecedent failure to apply the required constitutional standard before authorizing the screen on this record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation supply confrontation’s functional core and make any omission of Craig findings harmless—misreads what Coy and Maryland v. Craig actually require. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Craig treats those reliability features as necessary but not sufficient once the State affirmatively blocks face-to-face confrontation; the constitutional prerequisite is a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding tied to this child and trauma from the defendant’s presence, which Mississippi’s effectively automatic screen regime displaces. California v. Green and Kentucky v. Stincer do not alter that conclusion because they address different confrontation questions (prior statements and participation limits) and do not authorize dispensing with face-to-face confrontation without satisfying Craig’s predicate. Under a textualist/originalist approach attentive to separation of powers, we cannot allow legislative presumptions to substitute for the judicial findings the Constitution (as implemented by our precedent) demands before narrowing a core trial right.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor evidence preserved confrontation’s functional safeguards and that harmless-error review should apply—does not answer the distinct requirement in Coy and Maryland v. Craig: when the State affirmatively blocks face-to-face confrontation, the trial judge must make a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding tied to this child and trauma from the defendant’s presence. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasized, letting Mississippi’s regime operate as effectively automatic would convert Craig’s narrow exception into a categorical rule, undermining precedent and administrability and risking the Court’s legitimacy by appearing to dilute an explicit constitutional prerequisite through statute. Green and Stincer, which Alito invokes, concern different confrontation questions and cannot substitute for Craig’s mandatory predicate. Given the absence of the required finding at the time the right was denied, I am not persuaded that post hoc harmlessness can cure the failure to apply the correct constitutional standard on the record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmlessness-and-functionality point is the strongest counter: if oath, cross-examination, and demeanor were fully preserved, one might say the Clause’s practical protections were satisfied. But as the Chief Justice notes, Craig makes those features necessary but not sufficient once the State affirmatively denies face-to-face confrontation; the constitutional permission to depart from the text’s default turns on a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding tied to trauma from the defendant’s presence, which Mississippi’s effectively mandatory-by-request regime elides. That is not a mere technicality: under Coy and Craig, the individualized finding is the doctrinal gate that prevents a legislative presumption from displacing a core Sixth Amendment component. I therefore remain with the Petitioner; any harmless-error inquiry cannot substitute for the missing application of the constitutionally required standard on this record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation preserved confrontation’s functional core and thus any Craig defect can be treated as harmless—does not answer the procedural fairness problem Craig itself identified: reliability safeguards are necessary but not sufficient when the State affirmatively denies face-to-face confrontation without a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding. Chief Justice Roberts is right that a narrow reversal enforcing Craig’s predicate finding preserves both precedent and administrability by ensuring trial judges perform individualized gatekeeping rather than allowing a statute to function categorically. Even if California v. Green and Kentucky v. Stincer underscore cross-examination’s centrality, they address different confrontation questions and do not authorize dispensing with physical confrontation absent the Craig predicate. On this record, the absence of individualized findings is the constitutional error, and post hoc harmlessness cannot substitute for the required contemporaneous judicial determination.

John Roberts.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig make clear that denying face-to-face confrontation is permissible only upon case-specific, on-the-record findings that the particular child witness would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the procedure is necessary to protect the child. Treating Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) as effectively mandatory upon request—without individualized necessity findings tied to this child—conflicts with that constitutional prerequisite and risks converting Craig’s narrow exception into a categorical rule. While the State emphasizes the remaining confrontation elements (oath, cross-examination, demeanor), Craig held those features do not substitute for the required necessity finding when face-to-face confrontation is denied. Given the direct tension with this Court’s precedent and the need for a narrow correction to preserve institutional legitimacy and uniformity, I would vote to reverse.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s text guarantees an accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” which at the founding meant physical, face-to-face confrontation in open court. Coy v. Iowa held that placing a screen to block a child witness’s view of the defendant violates that core guarantee absent a case-specific showing; and Maryland v. Craig permitted only a narrow exception conditioned on individualized, on-the-record findings that the procedure is necessary to protect that particular child from trauma caused by the defendant’s presence. Mississippi’s statute, Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g), as applied here as a mandatory entitlement without such findings, substitutes a categorical legislative presumption for the constitutional prerequisite and therefore cannot be reconciled with the Confrontation Clause’s original meaning as enforced in Coy. Because the trial court failed to make the required individualized necessity findings, the confrontation right was denied and the conviction cannot stand on the theory that oath and cross-examination alone are “essential elements.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s core guarantees are oath, cross-examination, and the jury’s ability to observe demeanor, and those elements were preserved even with the screen in place, consistent with the functional understanding of confrontation reflected in cases like California v. Green and Kentucky v. Stincer. Although Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig emphasize that denial of face-to-face confrontation ordinarily requires a case-specific necessity determination, Craig also recognizes that protecting child witnesses from trauma can justify a limited departure from face-to-face confrontation where reliability safeguards remain. Here, the trial court’s use of Mississippi’s child-witness procedure, Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g), served a substantial state interest in protecting a very young child, and the State’s evidence of guilt—especially the recorded forensic interview and corroborating testimony—strongly supports harmlessness even if the findings were not as explicit as Craig would prefer. Given the practical consequences for prosecuting child-abuse offenses and the absence of any impairment of cross-examination, I would affirm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa holds that using a physical screen to block a child witness’s view of the defendant is an “obvious” violation of the Sixth Amendment’s face-to-face confrontation guarantee absent a constitutionally sufficient justification, and Maryland v. Craig permits such an exception only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding that the procedure is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child. Treating Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) as effectively mandatory—without individualized evidence and findings—substitutes a categorical legislative presumption for Craig’s required necessity determination, and that is not compatible with the Confrontation Clause as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment. The State’s reliance on oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation cannot cure the lack of the predicate finding Craig demands before dispensing with face-to-face confrontation. Because the record described does not show the required individualized necessity determination for this child, the conviction cannot stand on this procedure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa held that using a screen to prevent a child witness from seeing the defendant is a paradigmatic deprivation of face-to-face confrontation, and Maryland v. Craig permits that deprivation only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding that the measure is necessary to protect this particular child from trauma caused by the defendant’s presence. Mississippi’s use of a mandatory screen under Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g), without individualized findings tied to this witness, replaces Craig’s constitutional prerequisite with a categorical presumption and is therefore incompatible with the Sixth Amendment as applied through the Fourteenth. While the State emphasizes that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor evidence remained, Craig makes clear those elements do not suffice when the State dispenses with face-to-face confrontation absent the required necessity determination. Given the record’s lack of tailored evidence of trauma from seeing the defendant, the procedure cannot be upheld under Coy/Craig.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s text guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and Coy v. Iowa holds that this ordinarily means face-to-face confrontation, permitting exceptions only on a case-specific showing of necessity. Maryland v. Craig allows dispensing with face-to-face confrontation for a child witness only if the trial court makes individualized, on-the-record findings that the procedure is necessary to protect that particular child from trauma caused by the defendant’s presence; a mandatory screen regime under Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g), applied without such findings, contradicts that constitutional prerequisite. Maintaining oath, cross-examination, and jury observation cannot substitute for the distinct face-to-face component that Coy and Craig treat as the default constitutional command. Where Mississippi courts treat the screen as effectively automatic, they improperly displace a constitutional standard with a legislative presumption, and the resulting Confrontation Clause violation warrants relief absent a properly supported necessity determination.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause generally guarantees face-to-face confrontation, and Coy v. Iowa held that a screen specifically designed to block the child’s view of the defendant violates that right absent a constitutionally sufficient justification. Maryland v. Craig allows an exception for child witnesses only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding of necessity—after hearing evidence—that the procedure is needed to protect that particular child from trauma caused by the defendant’s presence, not via a categorical or mandatory statutory presumption such as Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) as applied here. If Mississippi courts treated the screen as effectively mandatory without individualized findings, that rule conflicts with Coy and Craig and is not a merely “procedural” variation preserving the “essential elements” of confrontation. Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s text guarantees an accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” which this Court has understood to include a presumptive right to face-to-face confrontation. Coy v. Iowa held that using a screen to block the witness’s view of the defendant is an “obvious” violation absent a constitutionally sufficient justification, and Maryland v. Craig permits dispensing with face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding of necessity after the trial court hears evidence that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence. A mandatory application of Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) (as described) that allows the screen whenever requested—without individualized findings—cannot satisfy Craig’s prerequisite and effectively substitutes a categorical legislative presumption for the judicial determination the Sixth Amendment requires. Because the error concerns the denial of face-to-face confrontation without the required necessity finding, the state court’s approach conflicts with clearly established precedent, warranting relief notwithstanding general assertions that other “elements” of confrontation were preserved.

Craig allows departure from face-to-face confrontation only when the trial court makes individualized, on-the-record findings that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence and that the procedure is necessary; a categorical, mandatory application of Miss. Even acknowledging the State’s interest in protecting child witnesses and the pragmatic benefits of trauma-reducing measures, procedural fairness requires the Craig findings before imposing a screen that eliminates direct visual confrontation. Because the record here lacked the required individualized necessity determination, the confrontation violation warrants relief notwithstanding the State’s harmlessness arguments.
